conversations.title: Woman With Dwarfism Opens Up About Dating, and the Behavior She Can’t Ignore
conversations.reply: The staring-then-stalling routine she describes, fascination first, real conversation never, turns up in account after account from women with visible disabilities. Naming it precisely is what actually shifts things, not another vague appeal to be kinder.

conversations.title: Parkinson's drastically changed how they have sex. They're not alone.
conversations.reply: Chronic illness reshaping how couples have sex is common enough to be unremarkable, yet it still gets whispered about like a confession rather than discussed like any other part of a long relationship. Silence here isn't tact, it's just another way disabled people's intimate lives go unaddressed.

conversations.title: Time to Pay Attention: This Is Bigger Than Any One Policy
conversations.reply: Disability rights rarely vanish in one vote, they get worn down clause by clause while people are told to be grateful for what's left. Every cut to transport and support narrows disabled people's social and dating lives long before anyone opens an app.

conversations.title: Disabled islanders urged to take part in survey
conversations.reply: A survey of disabled islanders' experience only matters if the results change something afterwards, rather than getting filed away next to the last one nobody acted on. What's missing on Jersey has rarely been data, it's follow-through.

conversations.title: Aurora proclamation of Disability Pride Month seen as part of efforts to better support residents with disabilities
conversations.reply: A mayoral proclamation reads well from outside a building disabled residents still can't get into. Disability Pride Month means little if the venues hosting the celebrations haven't fixed their own front step first.

conversations.title: Leeds Pride 2026 Set to Draw 60,000 as City Marks 20 Years of Celebration
conversations.reply: Sixty thousand people filling the city centre is the easy number to print; the harder question is whether the headline venues and afterparties let a wheelchair user through afterwards. An accessible route and an accessible nightlife scene are not the same achievement.

target: Roll with Cole and Charisma (interabled couple)
target_reply: Interabled couples like this keep getting asked the same reductive question, caregiver or partner, as though it has to be one or the other. Accounts from interabled relationships consistently show it is neither role that defines them, it is the relationship itself, still treated as a curiosity by everyone watching from outside it.

instagram_hitlist.who: Creators in interabled relationships or disabled people posting openly about their dating history on mainstream apps
instagram_hitlist.why: These accounts put the disclosure-then-disappear pattern in plain sight, which backs up the whole reason this account exists to argue against silence on the subject
instagram_hitlist.comment: That moment the replies just stop after disability comes up in the bio or the chat isn't rare, disabled daters have been naming that exact drop off for years and mainstream apps still pretend it's a coincidence.

instagram_hitlist.who: Manchester based access or nightlife accounts covering Gay Village venues, club nights or Pride events
instagram_hitlist.why: Direct line to the nightlife exclusion theme, particularly wherever an event brands itself inclusive without checking who can physically get in
instagram_hitlist.comment: An 'inclusive' night held somewhere a wheelchair user cannot get through the front door isn't inclusive, it's a headline event with a step nobody wants to mention out loud.

instagram_hitlist.who: #disabilitydating posts where someone is venting about being matched, chatted up and then ghosted on a mainstream app
instagram_hitlist.why: This hashtag is where the disclosure pattern gets described first hand, in the daters' own words rather than a third party summary
instagram_hitlist.comment: Match, chat, disappear the second disability is mentioned, disabled daters have been describing this exact sequence for years and it keeps getting rebranded as bad luck.

instagram_hitlist.who: #wheelchairlife posts documenting an access fail at a venue, bar or event, steps with no ramp, no step free entrance
instagram_hitlist.why: Grounds the venue exclusion argument in a real, specific access fail rather than a general complaint
instagram_hitlist.comment: Another night out that ends at a flight of steps nobody thought to check, and the venue still gets called welcoming to everyone.

instagram_hitlist.who: Access campaigners or heritage/accessibility consultants posting about a listed building refusing ramps or lifts
instagram_hitlist.why: Directly tests the historic building myth this account holds a hard line on
instagram_hitlist.comment: Somehow every 'you can't touch a listed building' claim survives right up until a ramp actually goes in, refusing reasonable access has never been about the bricks.

instagram_hitlist.who: #accessibility posts celebrating a genuine access win, step free entrance added, a ramp fitted, a venue that actually checked before promising access
instagram_hitlist.why: Where the celebration half of this account's position lives, proper recognition when access gets built properly
instagram_hitlist.comment: Step free entrance fitted and it actually works on the day, this is what every venue claiming to be accessible should have done from the start.
